transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hi, doctor. Thanks for seeing me. Um, I guess I came in because work is just getting... well, I teach high school, right? And I can sit down at my desk with a massive stack of essays or a new curriculum document, fully intending to just get it done and power through. 

Actually, they just changed the curriculum again this term. It's this whole new framework that honestly feels like a huge step backward for the kids. I was trying to explain that to the principal on Tuesday... or Wednesday? Tuesday, I think, because it was pouring rain and I left my umbrella in the staff room and got completely soaked walking to my car. I always buy those cheap umbrellas and they break instantly, I really need to just invest in a good one. 

But anyway, what was I... oh, right, the essays. So I sit down to work, and within like ten minutes I realize I’ve just been staring at the exact same page. I'll be thinking about three completely different things—like the umbrella, or what I need to get at the grocery store—and I'm barely taking in a single word of what’s actually right in front of me. So, yeah, that's why I'm here. It's becoming a real problem.
Over the past few weeks, when you're not trying to work on essays or documents, how has your overall mood been? Would you say you've been feeling down, sad, or empty most of the time?

No, I wouldn't say I've been feeling sad or empty or anything like that. I mean, I get frustrated with myself sometimes, obviously, but my mood is generally fine. Actually, I was just telling my sister the other day that I've been feeling pretty upbeat because the weather's finally starting to turn. We went hiking this past weekend up at Cedar Ridge, which was amazing. Have you ever been up there? The trails are great this time of year, before it gets too hot. We took her dog, a golden retriever mix, and he just loves the water up there. He actually chased a duck right into the lake and got covered in mud. It took us like an hour to clean out my car afterward, which reminds me I really need to get it detailed. The guy at the car wash down the street always tries to upsell me on the wax coating, and I never know if it's actually worth it or just a scam. But yeah, no, I'm not depressed or anything. Just... scattered, I guess.

When you were in school—say, elementary school through high school—did you ever have trouble paying attention in class or completing assignments, or were you someone who could focus pretty well back then?

Yeah, actually, it was kind of the same story back then. I mean, even in primary school, my report cards were always full of comments like "bright but careless" or "doesn't finish work unless closely supervised." It was basically a running joke in my family. My parents were constantly digging through my backpack and finding all these crumpled-up worksheets that I’d just completely forgotten to hand in. 

Which is funny, because now I'm the one handing out the worksheets. I try to make them digital whenever I can, though, because the school’s copier is a nightmare. It jams if you even look at it wrong. The history teacher, Mr. Davis—he's been there for like thirty years—he actually knows exactly how to smack the side of the machine to get it working again. It's like his secret superpower. He's retiring next year, and honestly, I don't know what we're going to do without him. We're planning this big retirement party for him, and I'm supposed to be organizing the catering, which I really need to get on. I was thinking maybe that local barbecue place? They did the end-of-year banquet last year and the brisket was incredible. 

But, um... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, school. Yeah, I definitely had trouble paying attention back then, too. Always kind of in my own world.

You mentioned having trouble focusing since elementary school. Has this been something that's affected you consistently across different situations—like reading for pleasure, watching movies, conversations with friends—or is it mainly when you're doing work-related tasks?

Well, it's definitely not just work stuff. I mean, I try to read for pleasure—I have this huge stack of books on my nightstand. Actually, I just bought a new one last week at that little independent bookstore downtown. Have you been there? The one with the green awning? The owner is so nice, she always remembers that I like sci-fi. She recommended this new space opera thing, and I was so excited to start it. I made myself a cup of tea—chamomile, because I was trying to wind down before bed. I usually get the loose leaf kind from the farmer's market, the guy there mixes it with lavender and it smells amazing. 

Anyway, I sat down with the book and my tea, and I read the first page... and then I realized I was thinking about whether I needed to renew my car registration. So I read the page again. And then I started wondering if the dog next door was going to bark all night again, because they leave him out in the yard and it's honestly so loud. I should probably talk to them about it, but I hate confrontation, you know? It's like when you have to tell a parent their kid is failing, it's just so awkward. 

So, yeah, reading is tough. Movies, too. If I'm watching a movie at home, I'm almost always scrolling on my phone at the same time, looking up the actors to see what else they've been in. Like, I was watching this old action movie the other day, and I spent half the time trying to figure out where I recognized the bad guy from. Turned out he was in a commercial for car insurance I saw like ten years ago. It's crazy how the brain holds onto stuff like that, right? 

But, wait... what was I saying? Oh, right, if it affects other things. Yeah, it's pretty much everything. Conversations, too. My friends will be telling me a story, and I'll just zone out and start thinking about something completely random, like what I'm going to have for lunch tomorrow. It's really embarrassing when they ask for my opinion and I have no idea what they just said.

When you're sitting at your desk or in meetings, do you find yourself fidgeting a lot—like tapping your fingers, bouncing your leg, or feeling like you need to get up and move around? Or do you tend to sit still pretty easily?

No, not really. I mean, I sit pretty still, I think. I'm not one of those people who's always bouncing their leg or tapping a pen. Actually, speaking of pens, I bought this really nice fountain pen a few weeks ago because I thought it would make grading papers more enjoyable. It's this deep blue color, almost like sapphire, and the ink flows so smoothly. I got it at that stationary shop in the mall. Have you seen the new food court they put in there? They have this amazing pretzel place now. I got one with jalapeño cheese dip last time I was there, and it was so good, though I ended up spilling a little bit on my shirt. It was my favorite shirt, too, the gray one with the subtle plaid pattern. I tried soaking it in club soda as soon as I got home, because my grandmother always swore by club soda for stains. She used to keep a whole crate of it in her pantry just for laundry emergencies. She was so particular about keeping things clean. Her house always smelled like lemon Pledge and fresh laundry. 

But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, fidgeting. Yeah, no, I don't really do that. I just sit there. I might be completely spaced out, but I'm sitting still while it happens.

When you're trying to focus on something but finding it hard to concentrate—like grading those essays—do you ever feel restless or have an urge to get up and do something else, even though you're sitting still?

Not really, no. I don't get that antsy feeling like I need to jump up or escape. I mostly just sit there staring at the paper while my mind goes somewhere else entirely. 

Speaking of those essays, though, my juniors just turned in their papers on the Industrial Revolution, and honestly, some of the sources they try to pass off are wild. One kid actually cited a website that claimed the steam engine was reverse-engineered from alien technology. I mean, I had to laugh. I showed it to Sarah, the earth science teacher, during our prep period. She is hilarious, and she always brings these amazing baked goods into the staff lounge. Last Tuesday she made these lemon blueberry scones with this little vanilla glaze on top, and they were incredible. I begged her for the recipe, but she said it’s a strict family secret that her grandmother brought over from Scotland. 

I’ve always wanted to visit Scotland, actually. The highlands just look so beautiful in all the pictures, and I'd love to try authentic haggis at least once, just to say I did it. I heard it's actually pretty good if you don't think too hard about what's in it, kind of like hot dogs, you know? My dad used to make us hot dogs every Saturday for lunch when I was a kid... 

Um, wait. I'm sorry, did I answer your question? What were we just talking about? Oh, right, feeling restless while grading. Yeah, no, I don't really get that urge to get up and move around. I just sit still and completely zone out.
Do you find yourself doing things without thinking them through first, or do you interrupt people when they're talking? Has anyone ever told you that you act too quickly or say things impulsively?

No, I don't think so. I'm actually pretty careful about thinking things through, maybe even too much sometimes. I definitely don't interrupt people, I hate when people do that. My brother-in-law is terrible about it. We were at dinner last Sunday—my sister made this incredible lasagna, by the way. She uses a mix of ground beef and Italian sausage, which I think is the secret. Plus she makes her own ricotta from scratch. She took this cheese-making class a few months ago at the community center, and she's been obsessed ever since. 

She actually tried to get me to take a pottery class with her there next month, but I don't know if I have the time. The school year is just getting so busy, and with parent-teacher conferences coming up... those are always so draining. You have to sit there and try to explain to parents why their kid isn't turning in assignments, and half the time they just want to argue about it. It’s exhausting. I usually have to go home and just lie on the couch for an hour in total silence to recover. 

But anyway... what was the question? Oh, acting without thinking. No, I don't really do that. I'm usually the one overthinking everything before I say it.

How much is this difficulty concentrating affecting your ability to do your job as a teacher? Are you worried about losing your position, or have there been any consequences at work because of these attention problems?

Well, it's actually getting pretty bad at work. The missed follow-through on things—like grading, entering attendance, responding to parent emails—it's become serious enough that my department chair actually put me on a support plan. Which is incredibly embarrassing, honestly. I've been teaching there for six years, and I've never had to be on a support plan before. 

It reminds me of when I was in high school and I had to be put on an academic probation plan for my math class. I was terrible at calculus. My teacher was Mr. Henderson, and he always wore these really loud, patterned ties. One time he wore a tie that had little cartoon frogs all over it, and I spent the entire class trying to count how many frogs there were instead of paying attention to the derivatives he was explaining. I think I counted forty-two frogs before the bell rang. 

I actually saw a frog in my garden just the other day. A little green tree frog, sitting right on one of my tomato plants. I was so proud of those tomatoes this year. I planted this heirloom variety called Cherokee Purple, and they grew huge. They make the best BLT sandwiches. My wife makes this incredible spicy mayo to go on them, with just a little bit of sriracha and lime juice... 

Wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, right, the support plan at work. Yeah, it's not just work, either. At home, my wife has started taking over all the bills and reminders and stuff, because she just can't count on me to keep track of them anymore. I kept forgetting to pay the water bill, and she finally just took all the passwords and set everything up on her own phone. It makes me feel awful, but I just kept dropping the ball.

When you were a kid—say, in elementary school or middle school—did teachers or your parents ever describe you as hyperactive, overly energetic, or as someone who was 'always on the go'? Or were you more the quiet type who just seemed to daydream a lot?

I was definitely not the hyperactive kid. I was way more of the quiet daydreamer type. I remember even back in primary school, my report cards always said the exact same things. It was always, you know, "he's bright but careless," or that I wouldn't finish my work unless I was closely supervised. And my parents were constantly finding these old, crumpled-up worksheets shoved at the very bottom of my backpack that I had just completely forgotten to turn in. 

I actually had this amazing Jurassic Park backpack in third grade that I kept all those crumpled papers in. It had the big T-Rex logo on it, and the bones actually glowed in the dark. I loved dinosaurs so much back then. I really wanted to be a paleontologist for a long time. My dad took me to the Field Museum in Chicago once, and seeing the Sue the T-Rex skeleton was just... mind-blowing. We took the Amtrak down there, which was an adventure on its own because the train broke down for like two hours just outside the city. We ended up playing Go Fish with this beat-up deck of cards my dad happened to have in his jacket pocket. He always carried the weirdest stuff in his pockets. Once he pulled out a tiny brass telescope at a baseball game...

Um, wait, sorry. I'm doing it again. What did you ask me? Oh, right, being hyperactive as a kid. Yeah, no, I wasn't bouncing off the walls or anything. I was just quiet, usually staring out the window, and completely forgetting that I had assignments to hand in.

The school year is just getting so busy, and with parent-teacher conferences coming up... those are always so draining. You have to sit there and try to explain to parents why their kid isn't turning in assignments, and half the time they just want to argue about it. It’s exhausting. I usually have to go home and just lie on the couch for an hour in total silence to recover. 

But anyway... what was the question? Oh, acting without thinking. No, I don't really do that. I'm usually the one overthinking everything before I say it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's inattention is accompanied by significant functional impairment or distress, and assess the severity/pervasiveness of the attention difficulties to help confirm ADHD diagnosis
doctor.question: How much is this difficulty concentrating affecting your ability to do your job as a teacher? Are you worried about losing your position, or have there been any consequences at work because of these attention problems?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: At work, the missed follow-through has become serious enough that my department chair put me on a support plan, and at home my wife has started taking over bills and reminders because she can’t count on me to keep track of them.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the consequences of my attention problems at work and how it affects my ability to do my job, which corresponds to the functional impairment criterion.

patient.answer:
Well, it's actually getting pretty bad at work. The missed follow-through on things—like grading, entering attendance, responding to parent emails—it's become serious enough that my department chair actually put me on a support plan. Which is incredibly embarrassing, honestly. I've been teaching there for six years, and I've never had to be on a support plan before. 

It reminds me of when I was in high school and I had to be put on an academic probation plan for my math class. I was terrible at calculus. My teacher was Mr. Henderson, and he always wore these really loud, patterned ties. One time he wore a tie that had little cartoon frogs all over it, and I spent the entire class trying to count how many frogs there were instead of paying attention to the derivatives he was explaining. I think I counted forty-two frogs before the bell rang. 

I actually saw a frog in my garden just the other day. A little green tree frog, sitting right on one of my tomato plants. I was so proud of those tomatoes this year. I planted this heirloom variety called Cherokee Purple, and they grew huge. They make the best BLT sandwiches. My wife makes this incredible spicy mayo to go on them, with just a little bit of sriracha and lime juice... 

Wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, right, the support plan at work. Yeah, it's not just work, either. At home, my wife has started taking over all the bills and reminders and stuff, because she just can't count on me to keep track of them anymore. I kept forgetting to pay the water bill, and she finally just took all the passwords and set everything up on her own phone. It makes me feel awful, but I just kept dropping the ball.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient meets criteria for ADHD Combined Type (requiring evidence of hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms) or ADHD Predominantly Inattentive Type. The patient shows clear inattentive symptoms since childhood and no impulsivity, but I need to clarify whether there are any hyperactivity symptoms I may have missed, particularly in childhood when ADHD hyperactivity is typically most prominent.
doctor.question: When you were a kid—say, in elementary school or middle school—did teachers or your parents ever describe you as hyperactive, overly energetic, or as someone who was 'always on the go'? Or were you more the quiet type who just seemed to daydream a lot?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even in primary school, my report cards said things like “bright but careless” and “doesn’t finish work unless closely supervised,” and my parents were always finding worksheets crumpled in my backpack that I had forgotten to turn in.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my behavior in childhood (elementary or middle school), specifically whether I had symptoms of hyperactivity or inattention back then, which corresponds to the requirement of symptom onset prior to age 12.

patient.answer:
I was definitely not the hyperactive kid. I was way more of the quiet daydreamer type. I remember even back in primary school, my report cards always said the exact same things. It was always, you know, "he's bright but careless," or that I wouldn't finish my work unless I was closely supervised. And my parents were constantly finding these old, crumpled-up worksheets shoved at the very bottom of my backpack that I had just completely forgotten to turn in. 

I actually had this amazing Jurassic Park backpack in third grade that I kept all those crumpled papers in. It had the big T-Rex logo on it, and the bones actually glowed in the dark. I loved dinosaurs so much back then. I really wanted to be a paleontologist for a long time. My dad took me to the Field Museum in Chicago once, and seeing the Sue the T-Rex skeleton was just... mind-blowing. We took the Amtrak down there, which was an adventure on its own because the train broke down for like two hours just outside the city. We ended up playing Go Fish with this beat-up deck of cards my dad happened to have in his jacket pocket. He always carried the weirdest stuff in his pockets. Once he pulled out a tiny brass telescope at a baseball game...

Um, wait, sorry. I'm doing it again. What did you ask me? Oh, right, being hyperactive as a kid. Yeah, no, I wasn't bouncing off the walls or anything. I was just quiet, usually staring out the window, and completely forgetting that I had assignments to hand in.

opening_question.intent: Establish rapport and identify the chief complaint that brings the patient to psychiatric evaluation
opening_question.question: Hello, I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent inattention across multiple contexts (work, reading, conversations, movies) since childhood, without significant hyperactivity or impulsivity symptoms. The pattern of 'bright but careless' reports, forgotten assignments, and current functional impairment (department support plan, wife managing bills) is consistent with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Inattentive Type. The absence of prominent hyperactivity or impulsivity, combined with lifelong inattention and current work/home dysfunction, supports F90.9 (ADHD, unspecified type) as the most appropriate diagnosis.
